What kinds of coins do you have?If you’re from America, you probably know about quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies. But have you heard of the half-dollar coin? On Ta’anis Esther, that’s the coin to use!

In the times of the Beis Hamikdash, it was a mitzvah for every Yid to give a half-shekel coin during the month of Adar. These shekalim would help pay for the צִיּבּור קָרְּבָנֹות (karbanos given on behalf of the entire nation, like the קָרְּבַן ּתָמִיד and מּוסַף קָרְּבַן) and other expenses of the Beis Hamikdash.

Nowadays, in order to remember this mitzvah, we also give a “half” coin to tzedaka—half of whatever type of money is used where we live. In America, it’s a half-dollar; in England, it’s 50 pence, etc. Our minhag is actually to give three of these “half” coins, since the Torah says the word “ּתְרּומָה—donation” three times when describing this mitzvah.

The Shulchan Aruch writes that from the age of 13, all Yidden should give machatzis hashekel. In תשנ”ב )1992(; during the last weekday sicha before Chof-Zayin Adar the Rebbe added that children who are younger than 13 should give machatzis hashekel, too! If possible, it should come from our own money.

Have you ever been to the Rebbe’s library near 770? If you go there, you might be able to see a Megilla written by the Rebbe Maharash himself! It has a different style than other Megillos. The Rebbe Maharash’s version shows us how a Megilla is to be written according to minhag Chabad.

Here are the differences: Some Megillos are arranged so that every column starts with the word “הַמֶלְֶך”. Chabad Megillos do not do that. Additionally, our Megillos have the ten sons of Haman written in regular size, not large letters that fill a whole column.

During the Megilla reading, we have the minhag to unroll our Megilla and fold it into three parts to look like an “אִגֶרֶת” (letter), as the pesukim describe it to be.

Haman’s name is found many, many times throughout the Megilla. Did you know that our minhag is not to make noise every time it’s written? Minhag Chabad is only to drown out Haman’s name when he is described with a title like “הָאַגָגִי—from King Agag”, or “הָרָע—the evil one”.

Sometimes, shaking our graggers by Haman’s name can get pretty noisy! Some people think that children shouldn’t come to kri’as haMegilla at all because their noisy graggers could disturb the reading. But the Rebbe says that children should come, and the noise from our graggers is a good thing! We just need to conduct the kri’ah in a way that everyone can still hear.

The Rebbe's advice is that each time Haman’s name is read, the person leining Megilla should pause and wait for everyone to finish making noise before continuing. This way, everyone will be able to clearly hear each word.

Are you ready to drown out Haman’s name with lots of noise and listen carefully to each word?

Another Purim mitzvah to make people happy is Matanos L’evyonim. We give tzedaka to at least two poor people. Since the money is meant to bring them joy on Purim, we don’t just put the money into a pushka. We either give it directly to poor people or to someone (or an organization) who will give it for us.

Purim is also a time to reach out to Yidden around us. The Rebbe explains that some people are poor because they don’t have money, and other people are poor because they don’t have knowledge. Besides giving Matanos L’evyonim money, it is also our job as chayolim to give ruchniyus’dik Matanos L’evyonim by helping

We go around to Yidden who don’t yet know about the mitzvos of Purim and help them to properly celebrate this holy day. This includes leining Megilla with them, inviting them to our se’uda, giving them Mishloach Manos to pass along to another Yid, or telling them about the mitzvah to give extra tzedaka. Let’s get out there and share the joy of Purim with others!

Did you know that this exciting mitzvah is not about getting Mishlo’ach Manos, but about giving them? The true purpose of Mishlo’ach Manos is to make other Yidden happy on Purim. We give at least two different types of food to at least one person. Boys give to boys, and girls give to girls. The Rebbe’s minhag was to give to a Kohen, a Levi, and a Yisrael. Think of how you can do this mitzvah in the most beautiful way. Perhaps you know someone who lives alone, or maybe a classmate who doesn’t have many friends? Imagine how happy they’ll be if you show up at their door with Mishlo’ach Manos! And that’s what this mitzvah is truly about.

The fourth mitzvah of Purim is to have a seuda. The Purim seuda is often so chayus’dik and long that people may forget to bentch. The Rema, the rav of Krakow, would go from house to house after seudas Purim and remind people to bentch for their meal.

(Learning from this, the Rebbe would end all of his farbrengens throughout the year with a reminder: “דִי וואָס דאַרפן מאַכן אַ בְּרָכָה ַ אַחֲרֹונָה, וֶועלן זִיכער מאַכן א ּבְרָכָה אַחֲרֹונָה—Whoever needs to say a bracha acharona will surely say a bracha acharona.”)

May this year’s seuda be full of chayus and joy. And remember to bentch!

Hooray! Purim is in the air! This Yom Tov is full of missions, between the four mitzvos of the day plus our

own Chabad minhagim. We give machatzis hashekel from the youngest age, we have a special way to write

and read the Megilla, we give Mishlo’ach Manos and Matanos L’evyonim properly and beautifully, have a seuda, dress up in holy themes, and go on mivtzoim. Let’s

learn all about how to celebrate Purim as Chassidim!

Further Reading: Kitzur Shulchan Aruch, 141:5; Sefer Haminhagim, p. 73; Sichos Kodesh 5738, vol. 1, pp. 582–

585; Sichos Kodesh 5752, vol. 2, p. 788; Sefer Hasichos 5702, pp. 82–83; Likkutei Sichos, vol. 31, pp. 279–280.
